definition: In computer vision, the inverse depth parametrization is a parametrization used in methods for 3D reconstruction from multiple images such as simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM).
details: Given a point p {\displaystyle \mathbf {p} } in 3D space observed by a monocular pinhole camera from multiple views, the inverse depth parametrization of the point's position is a 6D vector that encodes the optical centre of the camera c 0 {\displaystyle \mathbf {c} _{0}} when in first observed the point, and the position of the point along the ray passing through p {\displaystyle \mathbf {p} } and c 0 {\displaystyle \mathbf {c} _{0}} . Inverse depth parametrization generally improves numerical stability and allows to represent points with zero parallax. Moreover, the error associated to the observation of the point's position can be modelled with a Gaussian distribution when expressed in inverse depth. This is an important property required to apply methods, such as Kalman filters, that assume normality of the measurement error distribution. The major drawback is the larger memory consumption, since the dimensionality of the point's representation is doubled.

explainer.lead: Inverse depth parametrization encodes a 3D point observed by a monocular camera as a six-dimensional vector instead of raw coordinates. It matters because it generally improves numerical behaviour in SLAM and multi-image 3D reconstruction.

tiers.eli5: Instead of measuring how far away a point is, you describe the direction you first saw it from and how far along that line it sits.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use it with monocular pinhole cameras to encode points observed across multiple views; a pitfall is that it fixes the encoding to the camera centre of first observation.
tiers.paperLevel: For a 3D point p observed by a monocular pinhole camera from multiple views, a 6D vector encoding the optical centre c0 of the camera when the point was first observed and the point's position along the ray through p and c0; it generally improves numerical behavior.

explainer.example: A camera first sees a landmark from pose c0; rather than storing the landmark's XYZ coordinates, the system stores c0 plus where the landmark sits along the ray from c0 through the pixel.
